# Chronological Account of the Agent Failure

## Source Material

The reference is Anthropic's engineering blog post "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" by Justin Young, published Nov 26, 2025. The post describes failure patterns observed when Claude (specifically called out as Opus 4.5) runs on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows to tackle a long-horizon coding project. The post does not present a single trajectory with literal tool-by-tool transcripts; instead it describes recurring, reproducible patterns. The account below assembles those patterns into a chronological narrative of what the agent did.

## The Task

A user gives the Claude Agent SDK a single high-level prompt: **"build a clone of claude.ai."** The intent is a production-quality, full-stack web app. The harness used out of the box is the standard Claude Agent SDK, which already includes context management features such as compaction. The expectation going in is that, given compaction and a sufficiently capable frontier coding model, an agent looped across many context windows should be able to make continuous progress until the project is complete.

## Session 1 — The Agent Tries to "One-Shot" the App

In its first context window, Claude reads the high-level prompt and immediately attempts to build the entire app at once. The post describes this as the agent's tendency to "try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app."

The signal that something is wrong arrives not as an error from a tool, but as exhaustion of the context window itself: while implementing a feature, the model runs out of context. Compaction kicks in, but the post explicitly notes that compaction "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent." The result of the first session is a codebase containing a feature that is half-implemented and undocumented, with no structured record of what was attempted, what works, and what does not.

## Session 2 — The Successor Agent Has to Guess

A second context window starts. The new agent has no native memory of session 1; it inherits only whatever survived compaction plus whatever exists in the filesystem (which, in this baseline setup, does not include a progress file, a feature list, or an init script).

The agent's observable behavior in this session is to spend its time trying to reconstruct the project state — "guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again." Rather than making forward progress on new features, the session is largely consumed by re-deriving state that the previous agent had in its head but never wrote down. The signal of trouble here is implicit: the agent is burning tokens on archaeology instead of implementation.

## Later Sessions — Premature Victory

After enough sessions have run that some features actually exist in the repo, a different failure pattern emerges. The post describes it directly: "a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done."

The observable steps are: the agent inspects the repository, sees code that looks substantive, has no authoritative checklist that says otherwise (because none was created), and concludes the project is finished. It returns control without doing further work, despite the fact that, against the implied 200+ feature spec of a real claude.ai clone, the project is nowhere near complete.

## Within-Session Failure — Marking Features Complete Without End-to-End Testing

Independently of the cross-session problems, the post documents a per-feature failure mode. When working on an individual feature, Claude takes the following observable steps:

1. Makes code changes.
2. Performs some testing — specifically called out as "unit tests or curl commands against a development server."
3. Concludes that the feature is complete.

The signal Claude receives — unit-test passes and successful curl responses — is genuine but insufficient. As the post puts it, the agent "would fail recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end." Features were getting marked done while remaining broken from a real user's perspective.

The post notes that this improves once Claude is "explicitly prompted to use browser automation tools and do all testing as a human user would," using the Puppeteer MCP server. Even then, a residual failure remains: "Claude can't see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, and features relying on these modals tended to be buggier as a result" — i.e., the agent gets no visual signal back from native modals and so cannot detect that the feature is broken.

## The Final Outcome

The post does not present a single end-state for one specific run; it summarizes the aggregate outcome across the baseline (no special harness) setup: even Opus 4.5 looping on the Claude Agent SDK "will fall short of building a production-quality web app" from the "build a clone of claude.ai" prompt. The four observable failure outcomes are gathered into a table in the post:

1. Claude declares victory on the entire project too early.
2. Claude leaves the environment in a state with bugs or undocumented progress.
3. Claude marks features as done prematurely (without end-to-end testing).
4. Claude wastes time at the start of each session figuring out how to run the app.

These outcomes are what motivated the post's proposed two-agent harness (initializer agent + coding agent, with `init.sh`, `claude-progress.txt`, a JSON feature list, git commits per feature, and Puppeteer-based end-to-end testing).

Sources:
- [Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)

# Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents - Content Summary

**Published:** November 26, 2025 by Justin Young (Engineering at Anthropic)

## Core Problem

Long-running agents must operate in discrete sessions, with each new session starting fresh without memory of prior work. The author compares this to "a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift."

Even with context compaction, frontier models like Opus 4.5 running on the Claude Agent SDK fail when given high-level prompts like building "a clone of claude.ai."

## Two Failure Patterns Identified

1. **One-shotting attempts**: The agent tries to do too much at once, often running out of context mid-implementation, leaving features half-implemented and undocumented.
2. **Premature completion**: Later agent instances see partial progress and incorrectly "declare the job done."

## Two-Part Solution

1. **Initializer agent**: First session uses a specialized prompt to set up the environment, including:
   - An `init.sh` script
   - A `claude-progress.txt` file logging agent activity
   - An initial git commit showing added files

2. **Coding agent**: Subsequent sessions make incremental progress and leave structured updates. (Footnote clarifies these are "separate agents" only because of different initial user prompts—the system prompt, tools, and harness are identical.)
